turns.text: hey can i just think out loud for a sec. kind of a reflection thing, not a task
Of course. Go ahead and think out loud, and I'll listen and reflect things back if that helps. What's on your mind?

so i told my sister thao i might not do pharmacy. like im considering public health or nutrition for transfer instead

we got pho at pho ben thanh after her night shift on friday and i got kind of teary in the booth?? which is so dumb

It doesn't sound dumb. Saying something out loud for the first time, to someone you trust, over a warm bowl of soup after her shift, can bring up a lot at once. Relief, nerves, all of it. How did Thao react?

she was good about it. she said i should look up the bayshore program details so its not just a vague idea. which is.. practical, very thao

and honestly the digestion unit in anatomy is the best thing ive done all semester. like how nutrients get broken down and absorbed and why the gut does what it does, i could talk about it forever. i took like 4 pages of notes in all my colors

Four pages in all your colors says a lot. Your energy comes through when you describe how nutrients get broken down and absorbed. Looking up the program details could be a low-pressure way to see whether that interest holds up when you picture it as a whole field of study.

How did you feel once you'd said it and the teariness passed?

lighter i think. then kind of guilty

bc theres still the pharmacy talk and ive been putting it off forever

Lighter and guilty together makes sense. Telling one person made the idea real, and that makes the unfinished conversation feel heavier.

What happens when you picture it? Does something specific make you avoid it, like how she'll react, or not knowing what to say yet?

..idk

my dad's old radio is on my desk and i keep looking at it and wondering what he would think. i dont know why that matters so much

It makes sense that it matters. When you're deciding who you want to become, wondering what a parent who's gone would think is natural. You don't have to know his answer. It may just mean you want your choice to feel like something you can stand behind.

If the big talk feels like too much, you could start smaller. For example:
- Pick one low-stakes moment at dinner, not a sit-down.
- Open with something true and small, like "I've been really into the digestion unit in anatomy."
- Let the bigger conversation grow from that when you're ready.

Would it help to draft a couple of opening lines?
yes pls. short ones. ok im gonna eat now lol

Here are three short openers:

1. "Mom, the digestion unit in anatomy is my favorite thing I've learned this semester."
2. "I've been looking at other programs besides pharmacy, and I want to tell you about them."
3. "Can I talk to you about my transfer plans after dinner?"

Pick whichever feels most like you, and enjoy your food. ☕
